author: Tertullian
occasion: Tertullian writes to encourage and strengthen Christians who have been imprisoned for their faith and are awaiting possible martyrdom, providing spiritual nourishment to accompany the physical food supplied by the church.
argument: Tertullian urges imprisoned Christians to preserve the Holy Spirit's presence among them through peace and unity, since discord would give the devil a victory in his own house. He reframes the prison as a place of spiritual retreat rather than punishment, arguing that the world itself is a darker prison and that Christians have already renounced it. He presents their imprisonment as training for the spiritual contest of martyrdom, comparing it to the strict discipline of athletes and soldiers. He encourages the spirit to set before itself and the flesh examples of pagans who endured or even sought out bitter sufferings for earthly fame and glory. Finally, he argues that if people endure such things for vanity, through mental affliction, or merely through involuntary human misfortune, Christians should gladly endure them for truth and salvation.

outline.move: Tertullian offers spiritual food to the imprisoned Christians and urges them to preserve peace and unity so the Holy Spirit remains with them and the devil gains no foothold.
He reframes prison as a place of spiritual retreat, arguing that the world is a worse prison and that Christians lose little and gain much by their confinement.
He compares their imprisonment to the strict training of soldiers and athletes preparing for the contest of martyrdom under God as judge.
He urges the spirit to set before itself and the flesh examples of pagans, both men and women, who endured or sought out sword, fire, cross, beasts, and torture for earthly fame and glory.

He sets aside the motive of glory and observes that the same sufferings have been trampled underfoot even by affectation and a kind of mental disease, arguing that God permitted this both to exhort Christians now and to shame them on the final day if they fear to suffer for truth what others sought for vanity.

He turns to the common human condition, noting that people suffer fires, wild beasts, robbers, and enemies involuntarily, and argues that since everyone can endure such things for a human cause, Christians should not hesitate to endure them for God's cause.

cast.name: Tertullian
cast.who: The author, a Christian writer in Carthage, addressing imprisoned Christians.

cast.name: Lucretia
cast.who: A Roman woman who killed herself after being raped, cited as an example of endurance for honor.

cast.name: Mucius
cast.who: A Roman who burned his own right hand to demonstrate courage, cited as an example of endurance for fame.

cast.name: Heraclitus
cast.who: A philosopher who reportedly covered himself in dung and burned to death, cited as an example of voluntary suffering.

cast.name: Empedocles
cast.who: A philosopher who reportedly leaped into the fires of Mount Etna, cited as an example of voluntary suffering.

cast.name: Peregrinus
cast.who: A man who not long ago threw himself onto a pyre, cited as a recent contemporary example of voluntary suffering known to Tertullian's audience.

cast.name: Dido
cast.who: Queen of Carthage who chose death by fire rather than remarry, cited as an example of a woman enduring fire.

cast.name: Hasdrubal's wife
cast.who: The wife of Hasdrubal who threw herself and her children into the flames of burning Carthage, cited as an example of endurance.

cast.name: Regulus
cast.who: A Roman leader who, when captured by Carthaginians, refused to be exchanged for many Carthaginian captives, preferred to be handed back to the enemy, and was confined in a box-like structure studded with nails on all sides from the outside, feeling as many crosses.

cast.name: Cleopatra
cast.who: A woman who applied serpents to herself rather than fall into enemy hands, cited as an example of one who willingly sought out beasts—serpents more terrible than a bull or bear.

cast.name: The Athenian courtesan
cast.who: An unnamed Athenian woman who bit off her own tongue under torture rather than betray conspirators, cited as an example of endurance under torment.

voices.speaker: The devil (imagined speech)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'Non ergo dicat' (Let him not say), with his intended strategy presented as a mixture of direct first-person intent ('In meo sunt') and third-person description ('temptabo illos'), better understood as Tertullian's paraphrase of the devil's plan.

key_terms.sense: Christians who bear witness to their faith through imprisonment and potential death
The prison where the Christians are held, reframed as a place of spiritual retreat and training
The human spirit, contrasted with the flesh, and also the Holy Spirit dwelling with the imprisoned Christians
The weak human flesh, which must be strengthened by the spirit
The present world and its affairs, which Christians have renounced
The contest of martyrdom, presented as an athletic competition with God as judge
Earthly fame and honor that pagans sought through endurance, contrasted with heavenly glory
Voluntary pursuit of suffering out of vanity or mental disorder, contrasted with Christian endurance for truth
The prison reframed as a place of withdrawal from the world for spiritual purposes
The prison interpreted as a wrestling school or training ground for the contest of martyrdom
The prize of the contest, which is eternal life and angelic substance
The crown or wreath awarded to victors, used for both the corruptible crown of athletes and the eternal crown of martyrs

scripture: Tertullian quotes or alludes to Scripture using Old Latin or Vulgate forms. He cites the apostle Paul (1 Corinthians 9:25) and alludes to Matthew 6:21 ('where your heart is, there your treasure will be') and Matthew 26:41 ('the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak'). Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint/Vulgate tradition where applicable. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and chapter/verse numbers.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is approximate, based on the period of Tertullian's early Christian writings.
The identity of the Athenian courtesan is not given in the text.
The precise location of the imprisoned Christians is not stated in the text.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Regulus... was confined in a box-like structure studded with nails on all sides from the outside, feeling as many crosses
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: in arcae genus stipatus undique extrinsecus clavis transfixus tot cruces sensit
_unresolved_facts.fix: Regulus was confined in a kind of chest (arcae genus), packed in and pierced through on all sides from the outside by nails, feeling as many crosses (i.e., each nail caused pain like a cross)

_unresolved_facts.claim: Cleopatra... cited as an example of one who willingly sought out beasts—serpents more terrible than a bull or bear
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Bestias femina libens appetiit, et utique horridiores aspides serpentes tauro vel urso, quas Cleopatra immisit sibi
_unresolved_facts.fix: Cleopatra... cited as an example of a woman who willingly sought out beasts, and indeed serpents/asps more terrible than a bull or bear, which she applied to herself

_unresolved_facts.claim: The devil (imagined speech)... better understood as Tertullian's paraphrase of the devil's plan
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Non ergo dicat: In meo sunt, temptabo illos vilibus odiis, defectionibus aut inter se dissensionibus
_unresolved_facts.fix: The devil's imagined speech is introduced by 'Non ergo dicat' (Let him not say), with direct first-person speech ('In meo sunt, temptabo illos') — this is clearly marked as direct speech/quotation of what the devil might say, not merely paraphrase

_unresolved_facts.claim: He encourages the spirit to set before itself and the flesh examples of pagans who endured or even sought out bitter sufferings for earthly fame and glory
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: colloquatur spiritus cum carne de communi salute... spiritus contraponat sibi et carni acerba licet ista
_unresolved_facts.fix: He urges the spirit to converse with the flesh about their common salvation, and to set before itself and the flesh (contraponat sibi et carni) bitter things, though from many endured with equanimity, even sought out, for fame and glory's sake

_unresolved_facts.claim: He compares their imprisonment to the strict training of soldiers and athletes preparing for the contest of martyrdom under God as judge
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: agonothetes deus vivus est, xystarches spiritus sanctus
_unresolved_facts.fix: He compares their imprisonment to strict training of soldiers and athletes preparing for the contest of martyrdom under God as the president of the games (agonothetes), the Holy Spirit as the trainer (xystarches), with the crown of eternity and the prize of angelic substance
